title: Scheme representability of the stable abelian-level normalization
statement:
Let $k$ be any field, let $g\geq2$, and let $\ell\geq3$ be prime and different from $\operatorname{char}(k)$. Use the unpointed stable moduli stack $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,0}$, its smooth substack $\mathcal M_{g,0}$ and the smooth level scheme $L_{g,\ell}$ with the meanings in [def-sfb-stable-pointed-moduli-groupoids]. Let $Q_g$ be a coarse moduli scheme of $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,0}$. Normalize $\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,0}$ in the full level cover $L_{g,\ell}\to\mathcal M_{g,0}$, using all generic components. Explicitly, on a normal finite-type etale atlas $A\to\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,0}$, take the integral closure of $\mathcal O_A$ in the product of the function fields of $A^\circ\times_{\mathcal M_{g,0}} L_{g,\ell}$, where $A^\circ=A\times_{\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,0}}\mathcal M_{g,0}$; glue these normalizations and their descent arrows as a stack. The resulting normalization is represented by a $k$-scheme $Z_{g,\ell}$, with a morphism $a:Z_{g,\ell}\to\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,0}$ for which the induced scheme morphism $Z_{g,\ell}\to Q_g$ is finite. There is a 2-cartesian square
$$
\begin{array}{ccc}
L_{g,\ell}&\longrightarrow&Z_{g,\ell}\\
\downarrow&&\downarrow a\\
\mathcal M_{g,0}&\longrightarrow&\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,0}.
\end{array}
$$
Thus the inverse image of the smooth substack is exactly the original full level scheme. The word normalization means the integral-closure construction, not just an arbitrary finite cover. Finiteness is [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism]; fields, schemes and etaleness are [def-weil-field], [def-pc-scheme] and [def-weil-etale-morphism].

source.place: Sections 1.1 and 2.3.3--2.3.7, especially Proposition 2.3.4 and Remark 2.3.7; genus g >= 2 throughout. Local PDF WANTED; primary arXiv PDF read online.

proof.text: Put $\mathcal X=\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,0}$ and $U=\mathcal M_{g,0}$. The coarse-moduli theorem gives a smooth Deligne--Mumford stack, its coarse scheme $Q_g$, and the dense open $U$. The stable-isomorphism theorem supplies finite type and finite diagonal, which are not consequences of the definition of a moduli groupoid. Smooth level rigidification supplies the scheme $V=L_{g,\ell}$ and the representable finite etale surjection $V\to U$: on a test family its 2-fibre product is the actual frame scheme, with its isomorphism to that family. Thus all inputs of the finite-normalization theorem are available over the original field $k$.

source.place: Sections 2.3.3--2.3.7, especially the formal deformation and freeness argument of Proposition 2.3.6, printed pp.10--11; Stacks tags specified by the supporting nodes.

proof.text: Apply the finite-normalization theorem to $(\mathcal X,U,V)$. Denote the resulting normal Deligne--Mumford stack by $\mathcal N$ and its representable finite map by $\nu$. For every normal etale scheme atlas $T\to\mathcal X$, its pullback is exactly the integral closure in all generic field factors of $V\times_U(T\times_{\mathcal X}U)$. The etale compatibility identifies the two pullbacks on $T\times_{\mathcal X}T$ and supplies their descent arrows. This is the normalization construction specified in the item. The same theorem gives $\mathcal N\times_{\mathcal X}U\simeq V$ canonically over $U$. Let $k_0\subseteq k$ be the prime field. All moduli groupoids and frame covers in Step 1 are also defined over $k_0$, and their base changes are the indicated objects over $k$: on test schemes this is the same family, the same constant coefficient module, and the same frame, by base-change compatibility in smooth rigidification. The pullback of a frame is exactly the inverse-image frame followed by the degree-one base-change map specified in the current moduli-groupoid definition. Apply the construction over $k_0$ as well and call it $\mathcal N_0$. Since $k_0$ is perfect, the scalar-extension clause identifies $\mathcal N_0\times_{k_0}k$ with $\mathcal N$. We therefore check geometric automorphisms on $\mathcal N_0$ first.

source.place: Sections 2.3.3--2.3.7, especially the formal deformation and freeness argument of Proposition 2.3.6, printed pp.10--11; Stacks tags specified by the supporting nodes.

proof.text: Fix an arbitrary geometric object $y$ of $\mathcal N_0$ over an algebraically closed extension $\Omega/k_0$, and write $C=\nu_0(y)$. The versal-branch theorem supplies the complete deformation chart $[\operatorname{Spf}A/H]$ for $C$, where $H=\operatorname{Aut}_\Omega(C)$, with smooth locus obtained by inverting the product of its node parameters. Its finite algebra $B$ uses the full frame torsor, so it agrees with the algebra in the formal-chart compatibility of the normalization theorem. That compatibility identifies the completed neighbourhood above $C$ with $[\operatorname{Spf}B/H]$ and identifies $\operatorname{Aut}(y)$ with the stabilizer of a geometric closed point $b$ of $B$ over the closed point of $A$. By the versal-branch freeness assertion this stabilizer is $\{1\}$. Hence every geometric object of $\mathcal N_0$ has trivial automorphism group. The argument includes smooth $C$: then the parameter product is empty and equal to $1$. Here the perfect-field hypothesis of the formal-chart assertion holds because the ground field is $k_0$. An object of $\mathcal N$ over an algebraically closed extension of $k$ is, by the scalar-extension identification of Step 2, the same object of $\mathcal N_0$ with its fixed scalar map. Its automorphisms are unchanged. Thus the triviality also holds over the original $k$.

proof.text: Apply the inertia-free finite-cover criterion with target $\mathcal X$, source $\mathcal N$, and coarse scheme $Q_g$. The target has finite type and finite diagonal by the stable-isomorphism theorem; $\nu$ is representable finite by construction, and Step 3 establishes the required triviality at every geometric object. The criterion therefore represents $\mathcal N$ by a $k$-scheme $Z_{g,\ell}$ whose composite to $Q_g$ is finite. Under this equivalence $\nu$ is the desired morphism $a:Z_{g,\ell}\to\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,0}$. No restriction on the characteristic relative to the order of a stable curve's automorphism group was introduced.

source.place: Sections 2.3.3--2.3.7, especially the formal deformation and freeness argument of Proposition 2.3.6, printed pp.10--11; Stacks tags specified by the supporting nodes.

proof.text: The equivalence of Step 2 is over $U$, so the representing equivalence of Step 4 gives $Z_{g,\ell}\times_{\overline{\mathcal M}_{g,0}}\mathcal M_{g,0}\simeq L_{g,\ell}$. Unfold the current 2-fibre-product definition: over a test scheme an object is $(z,m,\phi)$, where $z$ is a point of $Z_{g,\ell}$, $m$ is a smooth family, and $\phi:a(z)\xrightarrow{\sim}m$ is an isomorphism of stable families. An arrow $(z,m,\phi)\to(z',m',\phi')$ is a pair $(v,w)$ satisfying $w\phi=\phi'a(v)$. Thus the equivalence includes the arrows and their compatibility with the specified isomorphism, and gives the asserted 2-cartesian square as fibred groupoids. Its smooth inverse image is the original full level cover, since Step 2 used every generic factor.
